mi_carney_crag_roped.blurb: The roped side of Carney Crag, on state forest land outside Iron Mountain in Michigan's Upper Peninsula, close to the Wisconsin line. The climbs are a mix of sport, top-rope and trad lines on firm, often blocky rock. Grades start easy and mostly sit between 5.6 and 5.10, with only a single 5.12 at the top end. Holds tend to be generous, which makes the crag a friendly place for newer climbers to get onto real rock. The bouldering has its own separate area close by, and the crag is also a popular spot just for hiking, so expect company on nice weekends.

mn_winona_sugar_loaf.blurb: A cone-shaped bluff on the edge of Winona, right beside Highway 61, whose profile was left by old quarrying. Roughly 85 feet of climbable rock carries a spread of bolted sport routes with stainless glue-in anchors that work for lowering and top-roping. Grades begin at 5.3 and reach the low 5.11s, with plenty of easy and moderate lines and a solid group of 5.10s, so beginners and stronger climbers both find something. The trail starts behind a building at the base and the hike up is steep, which can be rough on windy days. The top gives wide views over the river and town, and a man-made ice wall nearby brings crowds in winter.

mn_winter_wall.blurb: A steep, sun-warmed face on the south side of Barn Bluff (He Mni Can), the city-park bluff above the Mississippi at Red Wing. Nearly all of it is bolted sport climbing on pocketed dolomite, technical and sustained, with most lines between 5.11 and 5.13 and only a few easier ones. A handful of trad cracks add variety near the base. Rock quality is uneven: holds can break, rockfall is a real possibility under this stretch, and the stone stays damp after rain, so a helmet and a dry spell help. Sun-baked sections can run hot in summer.

mn_new_vice_area.blurb: One of the named sections of Barn Bluff (He Mni Can), the city-park bluff above the Mississippi at Red Wing. It is mostly bolted sport climbing on dolomite, with a few trad lines, a couple of top-ropes and two boulder problems. Grades center on 5.8 to 5.11, with 5.10 the most common, which makes it a gentler choice than the hardest walls elsewhere on the bluff. Rock here is pocketed and technical and can be loose, so a helmet makes sense, and the stone takes a while to dry after rain. Everyone hikes up from the trailhead at the base to reach the walls.

_expect.name: Louisville Swamp Boulder (S/W Twin Cities Metro, near Shakopee)

mn_louisville_swamp_boulder_s_w_twin_cit.blurb: A low-key bouldering outing inside Louisville Swamp, a wildlife refuge of old fields, savanna and floodplain southwest of the Twin Cities. The main attraction is a big bus-sized erratic standing alone in an open field, with a few smaller rock bands and an island of boulders elsewhere in the swamp. Problems run mostly V0 to V3 with a few harder ones, so it works as an easy introduction to outdoor bouldering. Water level decides the day: spring flooding and high river stages can turn the walk in into wading or cut it off entirely. Bugs and ticks are heavy in warm months, and landings are plain ground, so bring a pad.
mn_louisville_swamp_boulder_s_w_twin_cit.parking_note: Take 145th Street West off Highway 169 south of Shakopee, driving beyond the Renaissance Festival gate and across the rail crossing to reach the refuge lot, where several trails start. Some climbers instead stop short of the farm yard for a shorter walk, though that route floods more easily.

mn_north_little_foxx.blurb: The bouldering side of Little Foxx Canyon in West Duluth, built mostly around three tall, nearly vertical slabs plus a scatter of other boulders. The fine, grippy anorthosite rewards precise footwork and good friction. Many problems are high, though landings are decent, so expect to commit above your pad. Grades span from the easiest warm-ups up to V9, with the bulk falling between V0 and V4. The area feels wilder than its ten-minute distance from downtown suggests, and one trad crack sits among the boulders. Trails get you there from the road.
mn_north_little_foxx.parking_note: Drive up Haines Road from Skyline Parkway in West Duluth. The Superior Hiking Trail pull-off a short way along is the usual place to leave a car, and the climbing lies across the road from it.

mn_secret_lake_and_warmup_wall.blurb: Two crags in the remote Jeff's World cluster on the Minnesota-Ontario border, joined by one short trail off a channel running into David Lake. Reaching them takes a long paddle across several lakes, so a visit is a trip rather than a quick day at the crag. The climbing is mostly bolted sport with a few trad lines, on clean walls and slabs of modest height. Grades run from 5.7 to 5.13, but most routes sit between 5.10 and 5.12, so the Warmup Wall is not all easy. Some rock still wants cleaning, and the surrounding lakes add deep-water soloing options elsewhere in the region.

mn_brewer_s_park.blurb: A small city park in West Duluth, off Haines Road and shared with neighboring Bellevue Park, where urban bouldering mixes with a few roped climbs. Most of the climbing is boulder problems from the easiest grades up to V7, alongside several sport routes, a top-rope and a trad line, mostly in the 5.10 to 5.13 range. A stretch of the Superior Hiking Trail and miles of hiking and mountain-bike trails pass through, so the rock sits among everyday park traffic. Like much of Duluth, it offers boulders close to the road inside city limits.

mn_teacher_s_overlook.blurb: A bouldering stretch within Banning State Park along the Kettle River, beginning near the Teacher's Overlook picnic area and extending roughly half a mile down the river, below the Quarry Loop Trail. The sandstone is fine-grained with good holds, but it is porous and breaks easily when wet, so wait a couple of dry days after rain. Most problems sit on the river-valley cliff rather than free-standing blocks, with slabs, arêtes and some steep overhangs. The bulk fall between V0 and V3, with a few much harder lines. Landings vary and trails run past the base, so keep pads tidy. Late summer and fall are best, once biting insects and poison ivy ease off.

mn_casket_quarry_ice_mixed.blurb: A former quarry below Skyline Parkway in West Duluth, now part of Quarry Park and one of the best-known ice and mixed venues in the Midwest. Walls approach 100 feet, and seeping groundwater freezes down them each winter; volunteers also farm ice to extend the season. Most routes are bolted mixed lines from about M6 to M9, with a few ice climbs from WI3 to WI5. The summer rock is loose and exfoliating, so this is a winter destination, and the mixed lines want about a week of hard freeze to come into shape. Ice is usually firmest in December and January and softens in the late-February sun.
